17.1.6.4 SN2 Mechanism

The abbreviation SN2 stands for Substitution, Nucleophilic, bimolecular. It is a single step concerted mechanism, with bonds breaking and forming at the same time. The entering nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon atom of the substrate before the leaving group departs. The middle structure is a transition state, rather than an intermediate. The term bimolecular means that the transition state of the rate-limiting step (the only step in this reaction) involves the collision of two molecules (or ions).

This mechanism is generally followed by primary alkyl halides and methyl halides. For example, the reaction of hydroxide ion with methyl bromide to form methyl alcohol follow SN2 mechanism, shown below.

It is clear from the above one-step mechanism, that entering nucleophile can attack only from the back side because the front side is blocked by the halogen atom. In the transition state, carbon–bromine bond begins to break as the carbon–oxygen bond begins to form. In other words, the extent of bond formation on one side is equal to the extent of bond breaking on the other side.

This one-step mechanism is supported by kinetic information. The rate is found to double when the concentration of either reactant (nucleophile and substrate) is to be doubled. The reaction is, therefore, first order in each of the reactants and second order overall. The rate equation has the following form: rate = k [CH₃Br][⁻OH]

Back-side attack of nucleophile literally turns the tetrahedron of the carbon atom inside out. In the product, the nucleophile assumes a stereochemical position in space, opposite to the position of the leaving group originally occupied. This is called inversion of configuration at the carbon atom, shown in above reaction. SN2 mechanism is generally favored by polar aprotic solvents.

The type of mechanism followed by the secondary alkyl halides is governed by the nature of the solvent. If polar protic solvent is present, they follow SN1 mechanism, while in polar aprotic solvents, SN2 mechanism is followed.

17.1.7.2 E1 Mechanism

The abbreviation E1 stands for Elimination, unimolecular. The slow step of an E1 reaction is the same as in the SN1 reaction: unimolecular ionization to form a carbocation.

17.1.6.4 SN2 Mechanism

The abbreviation SN2 stands for Substitution, Nucleophilic, bimolecular. It is a single step concerted mechanism, with bonds breaking and forming at the same time. The entering nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon atom of the substrate before the leaving group departs. The middle structure is a transition state, rather than an intermediate. The term bimolecular means that the transition state of the rate-limiting step (the only step in this reaction) involves the collision of two molecules (or ions).

This mechanism is generally followed by primary alkyl halides and methyl halides. For example, the reaction of hydroxide ion with methyl bromide to form methyl alcohol follow SN2 mechanism, shown below.

It is clear from the above one-step mechanism, that entering nucleophile can attack only from the back side because the front side is blocked by the halogen atom. In the transition state, carbon–bromine bond begins to break as the carbon–oxygen bond begins to form. In other words, the extent of bond formation on one side is equal to the extent of bond breaking on the other side.

This one-step mechanism is supported by kinetic information. The rate is found to double when the concentration of either reactant (nucleophile and substrate) is to be doubled. The reaction is, therefore, first order in each of the reactants and second order overall. The rate equation has the following form: rate = k [CH₃Br][⁻OH]

Back-side attack of nucleophile literally turns the tetrahedron of the carbon atom inside out. In the product, the nucleophile assumes a stereochemical position in space, opposite to the position of the leaving group originally occupied. This is called inversion of configuration at the carbon atom, shown in above reaction. SN2 mechanism is generally favored by polar aprotic solvents.

The type of mechanism followed by the secondary alkyl halides is governed by the nature of the solvent. If polar protic solvent is present, they follow SN1 mechanism, while in polar aprotic solvents, SN2 mechanism is followed.

17.1.7 1,2-Elimination Reactions

17.1.7.1 Overview

We have already discussed that alkyl halides undergo substitution as well as elimination reactions in (Section 17.1.5). When treated with a strong base, an alkyl halide can undergo a type of elimination process, called 1,2-elimination, also known as β-elimination, in which a proton is removed from the β position, the halide is ejected as a leaving group from the α position and a double bond is formed between the α and β positions:

Alkyl halides undergo elimination reactions by two different types of mechanisms.

17.1.7.2 E1 Mechanism

The abbreviation E1 stands for Elimination, unimolecular. The mechanism is called unimolecular because the rate-limiting transition state involves a single molecule rather than a collision between two molecules. The slow step of an E1 reaction is the same as in the SN1 reaction: unimolecular ionization to form a carbocation.
